        About Me
        I grew up surrounded by nature and fascinated by wildlife: the variety of shapes, colors, and sounds, and the fact that so many species manage to coexist and occupy different niches in the same ecosystem. At some point, that fascination began to mix with concern. Habitats are changing faster than most people realize, and so is the wildlife within them.
        That tension is what led me to conservation biology. Protecting biodiversity is not just about caring deeply; it requires generating the right evidence, at the right scale, in time for people to act on it, and working with land managers, local communities, and policymakers to make sure it is understood, trusted, and actually used.
        I see myself as a mix between an ecologist and a conservation biologist with a particular interest in understanding how environmental change and human activities shape biodiversity, and why some populations and species are more vulnerable than others. I combine non-invasive biodiversity monitoring, especially bioacoustics and camera trapping, with field experiments and ecological modeling to study these questions in temperate and tropical forests, from working pine forests in the U.S. Southeast to the Amazon, the Atlantic Forest, and Central Africa.

    Research
    My research asks why some species and communities persist in the face of environmental change and human activities while others decline. My projects span tropical and temperate systems, from tropical forests in the Amazon and the Congo Basin to working pine forests in the U.S. Southeast, but they share a common goal: generating biodiversity data that is rigorous, scalable, and actionable.

    
      
        📍Amazonian Rainforest, Peru
        Biodiversity Responses to Liana Thinning
        Liana thinning is promoted as a nature-based climate solution to increase carbon sequestration in selectively logged tropical forests, but what does it mean for the wildlife that live there? In collaboration with Conservation International and Peruvian researchers, we are conducting a field experiment assessing how this practice reshapes vertebrate communities.
        Learn more
      
      
      
        📍Congo Basin Rainforest, Gabon
        Forest Certification, Human Activities, and Vertebrate Community Assembly
        Does forest certification protect biodiversity in the Congo Basin? Through passive acoustic monitoring and AI-driven species identifications, we examine how logging history, local forest conditions, and certification status shape bird and primate communities in Gabonese forests.
      

      
        📍Intact Forests, Global
        Soundscape Baselines for Intact Forests
        How do we know what a healthy forest sounds like, and how do we detect when it starts to change? Together with a network of local scientists, conservationists, and community partners, we are establishing biodiversity baselines in some of the world's most intact forests through the Sound Forest Lab.
        Learn more
      

      
        📍Atlantic Forest, Paraguay
        Soundscapes of the Tapytá Natural Reserve
        What can sound tell us about biodiversity in one of the most fragmented forests in South America? With the Moisés Bertoni Foundation and the Universidad Nacional de Asunción, this project uses passive acoustic monitoring and AI to map biodiversity across the Tapytá Reserve in Paraguay's Atlantic Forest.
        Learn more
      

      
        📍Southeastern Coastal Plain, USA
        Winter Foraging Ecology of Bats in Working Forests
        Forest management plays a key role in conserving forest landscapes and preventing their conversion to other land uses in southeastern US Coastal Plain. Many bats remain active through winter in the managed forests of the southeastern U.S., and my dissertation examined how forest management shapes their winter habitat use and foraging, a season and landscape that had been largely overlooked.
        Read dissertation
